one_liner: Rust SIMD image-resize crate (SSE4.1/AVX2/NEON/wasm); with AVX2 it is 1.3-1.6x faster than libvips and about 10x faster than the image/resize crates.
what_it_does: fast_image_resize downscales and upscales images held in memory: 8-bit, 16-bit and f32 pixels with 1-4 components, plus i32 grey. It offers Nearest, separable convolution (Box, Bilinear, Hamming, CatmullRom, Mitchell, Gaussian, Lanczos3, custom), fixed-kernel interpolation and super-sampling. The API is a reusable Resizer whose resize(src, dst, options) writes into a caller-allocated destination; options cover cropping, fit-into-destination and alpha premultiply/unpremultiply. It accepts its own Image/ImageView types and, with the 'image' feature, image-rs DynamicImage and some ImageBuffer types. It does no decoding or encoding, and there is no C ABI: C++ callers need their own FFI shim (the Python package cykooz.resizer wraps it for Python).
how_it_is_fast: It uses the Pillow-SIMD approach (the source says so): weights for each output pixel are precomputed once per resize as an adaptive-size kernel and quantized to i16 fixed point, with the precision chosen per filter so sums fit in i32. Separable passes then run as multiply-add kernels (_mm256_madd_epi16 plus byte shuffles on AVX2, with equivalent SSE4.1, NEON and wasm SIMD128 paths). For u8 images the vertical pass runs first over only the source columns the horizontal kernel will touch. 4-row blocking is used in the horizontal pass. The CPU extension is detected at run time and can be forced with an unsafe setter. Alpha premultiply and divide are separate SIMD passes, and an optional rayon feature splits the work across threads.
when_to_use: Rust services that make thumbnails or previews: downscaling large 8-bit RGB/RGBA photos on x86-64 with AVX2, where it beats the image crate by about 13x and the resize crate by about 10x at Lanczos3.
Replacing a single-threaded libvips reduce in a Rust pipeline on AVX2 machines: RGB8 Lanczos3 13.52 vs 17.31 ms, Bilinear 3.55 vs 5.58 ms, L8 Lanczos3 4.26 vs 12.54 ms on a Ryzen 9 5950X.

16-bit, f32 or alpha formats (RGBA16, LA8, RGBA32F) where the integer and float SIMD kernels have a larger lead over libvips (RGBA16 Lanczos3 53.51 vs 345.06 ms), with the caveat that libvips' alpha path in this harness runs in float.
WebAssembly or no_std targets that need SIMD resizing without a C dependency (wasm32 SIMD128 paths; the 'no_std' feature since 6.0.0).
when_not_to_use: C or C++ codebases: there is no C API, and the margin over libvips (C, with C++ bindings) on RGB8 is only 1.3-1.6x with AVX2.

CPUs without AVX2: with only SSE4.1, libvips is faster on RGB8 Bilinear (5.58 vs 5.83 ms) and Bicubic (9.92 vs 10.34 ms). On an ARM Neoverse-N1, libvips wins RGB8 Bilinear (26.85 vs 29.21 ms) and fir's NEON Lanczos3 lead is about 1.1x (79.72 vs 87.42 ms).
Targets with no SIMD path: the portable 'fir rust' path is about 2x slower than libvips on RGB8 (Lanczos3 37.26 vs 17.31 ms), and f32 has no NEON or wasm path in the released 6.1.0.
Gamma-correct resizing out of the box: it filters stored values (for example sRGB) directly; linearize with PixelComponentMapper (create_srgb_mapper) first and pay for the extra passes.
Full image pipelines (decode, colour management, sharpen, encode): this crate only resamples.

integration.dependencies: cfg-if, num-traits, thiserror (plus document-features under std); optional image, bytemuck, rayon, and cpufeatures for no_std
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.87 (rust-version in Cargo.toml); avoid Rust 1.95-1.96 for wasm32 SIMD128 builds (an LLVM regression breaks U8x4 alpha division, per the README)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE4.1 and AVX2 detected at run time), aarch64 (NEON), wasm32 (SIMD128), portable Rust fallback elsewhere; std or no_std
integration.thread_safety: Resizer::resize takes &mut self and keeps internal scratch buffers, so use one Resizer per thread; the 'rayon' feature parallelizes a single resize internally.

gotchas: ResizeOptions defaults to premultiplying and dividing by alpha for alpha formats, which nearly doubles RGBA8 Lanczos3 time (24.08 vs 13.52 ms for RGB8); call use_alpha(false) for opaque or already-premultiplied data.
Resizer::set_cpu_extensions is unsafe: forcing AVX2 or NEON on a CPU without it is undefined behaviour.

Version 6.0.0 made 'std' a default feature (5.6.0 was yanked for the same break), so default-features = false users must add 'std' or 'no_std' explicitly. Before 6.1.0, a one-thread rayon pool could deadlock on ResizeAlg::Nearest.
Past SIMD alpha-division bugs (NEON U8x2 multiply in 5.1.3, SSE4.1/AVX2/NEON U16x2 and NEON U16x4 divide in 5.1.4) were fixed in point releases; pin a recent version if you resize LA/LA16 images.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Pillow-SIMD (whose C convolution design it ports) and libvips when you are in Rust or wasm and want a dependency-free crate with AVX2, NEON and SIMD128 kernels for 8-bit, 16-bit and f32 pixels. In C or C++, stb-image-resize-opt, Skia or libvips avoid an FFI shim, and tir (tinyexr) is the closer fit for f32 HDR resizing.
verified_claims_summary: The author's criterion benches (mean point estimate, single thread, release profile opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu, Rust 1.97.1, Ryzen 9 5950X, Ubuntu 24.04) resize a 4928x3279 photo to 852x567. RGB8 Lanczos3 takes 13.52 ms with AVX2, against 17.31 ms for libvips 8.15.1 (Ubuntu package, concurrency 1, cache off), 176.09 ms for image 0.25.6 and 137.70 ms for resize 0.8.9: 1.28x, 13x and 10x (derived from page data). The RGBA8 and Box margins over libvips are not like for like: libvips premultiplies into float for alpha, and its Box row is not a box filter. No correctness bug was found behind the numbers.
status_note: Actively maintained by one author (6.1.0 on 2026-07-21, last commit 2026-08-20, with wasm f32 SIMD unreleased), dual MIT/Apache-2.0, 463 stars, about 20.4 million crates.io downloads and 128 reverse dependencies, 2 open issues and every bug-labelled issue closed.
measurement_notes: For the orchestrator, no correctness bug found; the A tier holds for the RGB8/L8 convolution rows. (1) The libvips 'Box' row should not be cited. The harness times ops::shrink. In libvips 8.15.1 (shrink.c), vips_shrink with non-integer factors (here about 5.78) calls vips_reducev and vips_reduceh with gap 1.0. Per reduceh.cpp, that is an integer box pre-shrink by 5 followed by the default Lanczos3 reduce of the remainder: not a box filter, and not the same work as fir's Box convolution. That is why the libvips Box time (61.51 ms) exceeds its own Lanczos3 time (17.31 ms), and the 23x Box ratio is a harness artifact. (2) The lead over libvips depends on AVX2. With fir forced to SSE4.1, libvips wins RGB8 Bilinear (5.58 vs 5.83 ms) and Bicubic (9.92 vs 10.34 ms). On arm64 (Neoverse-N1, benchmarks-arm64.md), libvips wins RGB8 Bilinear (26.85 vs 29.21 ms), and fir NEON leads Lanczos3 by about 1.10x (79.72 vs 87.42 ms). (3) dev.md documents RESULTS_LIFETIME, which reuses the image, resize and libvips rows from earlier runs (up to N days old) while always re-running fir. The page does not say whether that was used, so its competitor rows may come from an older run than the fir rows. (4) Timed loops differ: the resize crate builds its resizer and coefficients outside the timed closure, fir recomputes coefficients on every call, and image and libvips allocate their output on every call. The reported figure is criterion's mean, not the median.
